proof_steps.title: Definitions, original target, and premise adapter
proof_steps.body_md:
For nonempty S the author claims
$I(S)=\sum_{\kappa\in Q_S}D^\kappa v(r)\prod_{i\in S}(x_i-r_i)^{\kappa_i}/\kappa!$,
where $Q_S$ consists of multiindices positive on S and zero elsewhere. Define this right-hand side as $\widetilde I(S)$ and set $\widetilde I(\varnothing)=0$. Group every masked Taylor expansion by its nonzero-coordinate support to obtain $v(x_S)=b+\sum_{T\subseteq S}\widetilde I(T)$, then invoke coefficient uniqueness for all masks, including the empty mask. A single full-input equality cannot establish uniqueness.
A smooth function need not equal its Taylor series: $v(t)=e^{-1/t^2}$ for nonzero t and $v(0)=0$ has all derivatives zero at 0, but $I(\{1\})=e^{-1}$. This refutes the unrestricted smooth-function reading; adding analyticity would change the original proposition. If Eq. (2) is instead a given valid Taylor representation, that example does not satisfy it and does not refute the conditional grouping argument. It also does not satisfy the global high-order zero-derivative Assumption 1-β, so it does not refute the next finite-order implication. The original formula and proof are retained.

proof_steps.title: Classical mixed partials and their existence order
proof_steps.body_md:
Fix $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $v:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, x, and r. A mask keeps x_i on A and r_i elsewhere. Set $g(A)=v(x_A)$, $b=g(\varnothing)$, and $g_0=g-b$. The source interaction is $I_{g_0}$, so its empty value is zero. Let e_i be a coordinate unit vector and $a_i=x_i-r_i$.
The classical partial is $D_i f(z)=\left.\frac d{dt}f(z+t e_i)\right|_{t=0}$. Encode a multiindex by a nondecreasing coordinate list $(i_1,\ldots,i_q)$, and define $P_0=v$, $P_j=D_{i_j}P_{j-1}$. Classical existence of the stated mixed partials includes actual differentiability of each required prefix along the next coordinate, and 1-β gives $P_q\equiv0$. These existence conditions and the zero value are encoded together; only lists q>M are used. No extra global smoothness of all low derivatives is assumed. C1 alone does not imply existence of high derivatives. A fixed ascending order is used; a reverse convention can use the same difference argument in reverse order, without interchanging mixed partials.

proof_steps.title: Commutation of finite differences and true partial derivatives
proof_steps.body_md: Define $\delta_{a,i}f(z)=f(z+a e_i)-f(z)$. If f is differentiable along coordinate i everywhere, its finitely many translated sums and differences are too. Translation gives $D_i(f(\cdot+h))(z)=D_i f(z+h)$ because $(z+t e_i)+h=(z+h)+t e_i$. The one-variable difference rule yields $D_i(\delta_{a,j}f)=\delta_{a,j}(D_i f)$. Induction extends this to arbitrary finite rectangular differences. Only translations and finite additions are used, with no infinite series or higher directional chain rule.

proof_steps.title: Zero mixed partials imply zero rectangular differences
proof_steps.body_md: Induct on the direction-list length q, allowing arbitrary directions and real steps. For the empty list, both the difference and the order-zero partial are f, and its assumed zero value proves the claim. For a nonempty list, let R denote the remaining differences. The prefix-existence premise applies the induction hypothesis to $D_{i_1}f$, giving $R(D_{i_1}f)=0$. Commutation then gives $D_{i_1}(Rf)=0$. For fixed z, $H(t)=(Rf)(z+t e_{i_1})$ is differentiable on the whole real line with zero derivative. The mean value theorem gives $H(a_{i_1})=H(0)$, so the full rectangular difference is zero. Negative and zero steps require no new restrictions.

proof_steps.title: Bridge from rectangular differences to actual coordinate masks
proof_steps.body_md: List the distinct coordinates of S, take steps $a_i=x_i-r_i$, and start at r. Induct on that list. The empty difference is $v(r)=g(\varnothing)$. Adding a previously absent coordinate splits the rectangle into its translated and untranslated parts. On every remaining subset U, the translated vector is exactly the mask for $U\cup\{i\}$ and the untranslated vector is the mask for U. Subtracting the alternating sums is the insertion identity for $I_g(S)$. This bridge holds for an arbitrary model v; no polynomial representation is assumed.

proof_steps.title: Complete finite-difference induction

The induction hypothesis quantifies over arbitrary coefficient functions and n, so it yields a₁,…,a_$M=0$. Substitute into the first row to obtain a₀=0. Finally take a₀=0 and $a_k=w_k/\binom nk$; positive denominators recover w_k=0. `Harsanyi.Sparsity.binomial_matrix_kernel` proves the general statement, not a few fixed matrices.

proof_steps.title: Infinite parameter family and sign partition
proof_steps.body_md: For $n\ge3$ with $n\equiv2,3\pmod4$, let $q=\binom n2=n(n-1)/2$. It is odd: at $n=4j+2$ it is $(2j+1)(4j+1)$, and at $n=4j+3$ it is $(4j+3)(2j+1)$. In particular $n=4j+3$ is infinite. Partition the q pairs into a positive family P of size $(q-1)/2$ and a negative family Q of size $(q+1)/2$. Such finite subsets exist. Set c_A=1 on P and −1 on Q, so the pair coefficients sum to −1.

proof_steps.title: Actual model and all interaction coefficients
proof_steps.body_md: Use $x=(1,\ldots,1)$, $r=0$, and the smooth quadratic model $v_n(z)=\sum_i z_i+\sum_{|A|=2}c_A\prod_{i\in A}z_i$. Its output baseline is zero. Pure-AND coefficient distribution and linearity give singleton interactions 1, pair interactions c_A, and all other interactions zero. Thus $A^{(1)}=n$ and $A^{(2)}=-1$. proof_steps.title: Check the original three assumptions
proof_steps.body_md: Take $M=2<n$. All global mixed derivatives of total order at least 3 vanish, proving even 1-β; the displayed coefficients give 1-α directly. A fixed pair is contained in a uniform m-element mask with probability choose(m,2)/q, so $\mu_m=m-\binom m2/q$ for $0\le m\le n$. Its increment is $1-m/q\ge1-2/n>0$, proving Assumption 2. For m≥1, $\mu_m/m=1-(m-1)/(2q)$ is nonincreasing, so $\mu_{m\prime}\ge(m\prime/m)\mu_m$ for $1\le m\prime\le m$. At $m\prime=0$ both sides are zero. Assumption 3 holds with the fixed p=1.

The cancellation magnitude 2/[n(n−1)] decays polynomially, and $n|\eta|\to0$ places the example in the nearly canceling Case 2. Nevertheless $R^{(2)}/\binom n2=1$ always.

sparse-issue-asymptotic-sparsity.title: Polynomial cancellation does not imply same-order sparsity

Assign second-order coefficients $\pm1$ with counts $(q-1)/2$ and $(q+1)/2$, giving total $-1$. The model $v(z)=\sum_i z_i+\sum_{|A|=2}c_A\prod_{i\in A}z_i$ at the all-one input and zero baseline has $A^{(1)}=n,A^{(2)}=-1$ and zero higher interactions and mixed derivatives. Its order mean is $\mu_m=m-\binom m2/q$; the increments are $1-m/q>0$, and $\mu_m/m=1-(m-1)/(2q)$ is nonincreasing. The original three assumptions hold with $M=2,p=1$. With fixed $\tau=1/100$, $R^{(2)}=q$ and $\eta^{(2)}=-1/q$, polynomially small despite every second-order term being salient. Theorem 3’s bound $100q$ still holds.
